BALA KANDA 
The following day, baving fulfilled the traditional rites, King 
Dasaratha gave away innumerable cows in charity. On behalf of 
each of his sons, be bestowed on the brahmins thousands of cows 
whose horns were covered with gold, yielding rich milk, together 
with their calves. 
With every cow the king gave away a metal 
milking vessel. 
On that day, four hundred thousand cows 
were given away by him. That mighty king holding his sons 
supremely dear, gave incalculable wealth in their name. King 
Dasaratha, performing these deeds of charity, surrounded by 
his sons, resembled Brahma attended by the Regents of the world. 
CHAPTER 73 
Th8 marriage ceremonies are completed 
ON tbe day on which King Dasaratha distributed the cows in 
charity, the grest bero Yudbajit, the son of the King Kaikeya 
and the maternal uncle of Bbarata, also came to Janaka's 
capital. 
Seeing King Dasaratha, he made enquiries as to his welfare 
and said : " 0 King, the Lord of Kaikeya, through a1fection, 
sends tidings of his well-being to thee, and seeks to know if it be 
well with thy friends. 0 Great King, my father desired to see 
Prince Bbarata, and for this purpose I went to Ayodhya. There, 
hearing that thou badst gone to Mithila with thy sons, for their 
nuptials, I came hither in baste to see the son of my sister."' 
King Dasaratha thereupon duly honoured his kinsman who 
spent the night happily in company with the princes. 
The following day, rising early, King Dasaratha performing 
his customary devotions, proceeded to the sacrificial pavilion, 
escorted by the sages. 
At an auspicious hour in the presence of Shri Vaaishtha and 
other sages, Shri Ramachandra and his brothers adorned with 
every ornament being present, the preliminary ceremonia were 
performed.

brief.summary_1line: Dasaratha gives vast charity, Janaka hosts the rites, and Sita is formally married to Rama before sages and the sacred fire.

image_candidates.scene_text: King Janaka places Sita's hand into Rama's as they sit before the blazing sacrificial fire in the flower-decorated pavilion.
As the wedding is declared, flowers rain from the sky while the gods cry 'Jai!' above the gathered sages and kings.
Rows of richly adorned cows with gold-covered horns stand beside metal milking vessels as King Dasaratha gives them away in charity.

deep.rich_summary: After the arrival of King Dasaratha in Mithila for the weddings of his sons, he performs lavish acts of charity, donating hundreds of thousands of richly adorned cows to the brahmins in their names. Bharata’s maternal uncle Yudhajit arrives from the Kaikeya kingdom and is warmly received. The next day, the royal and sage assemblies gather in the marriage pavilion where Vasistha, Vishwamitra, and other rishis prepare the sacred fire and ritual implements. King Janaka formally offers his daughter Sita to Rama, declaring that she will accompany him in virtue and devotion. When Rama accepts her hand, the marriage is sanctified by Vedic rites. The moment is celebrated not only by those present but by the heavens themselves: divine music resounds and flowers rain from the sky, marking the sacred union of Rama and Sita.

highlight_spans.why: Dasaratha’s immense charity—hundreds of thousands of cows—shows royal dharma and the grandeur surrounding the marriages.
Janaka’s welcoming declaration that Dasaratha needs no permission to enter frames the wedding as a union of families and kingdoms.
Janaka’s emotional words offering Sita to Rama highlight the tenderness and gravity of the moment.
The climax of the chapter: Sita and Rama are joined in marriage and the gods celebrate with divine music and a shower of flowers.

top_scenes.scene_text: Sita and Rama sit before the blazing sacrificial fire as King Janaka joins their hands while celestial flowers rain down and divine music fills the sky.
Vasistha lights the sacred fire in the marriage pavilion while Vishwamitra and other sages decorate the altar with flowers, incense, and golden vessels.
King Dasaratha ceremonially donates vast herds of gold-horned cows with calves and vessels to brahmins, surrounded by his sons like Brahma among the gods.
